Fit expected counts with structural zeros by iterative proportional fitting

Source: R/ipf.R
lsa_ipf.Rd

lsa_ipf() fits the expected counts of a count table with structural zeros by iterative proportional fitting. When some transitions cannot occur by construction (structural zeros, such as self-transitions in a coding scheme that merges repeated codes), the quasi-independence model fits expected counts that are zero in the forbidden cells and reproduce the observed row and column totals; it has no closed form and is found by iterative proportional fitting (Wickens, 1989), which rescales the rows and columns of the table in turn until both sets of totals match. Under ordinary independence, the expected count of a transition is the product of its row and column totals divided by the grand total, a formula that assigns expected counts to impossible cells.

lsa() calls lsa_ipf() when loops = FALSE or structural_zeros is given, so it is needed directly only to inspect the expected table or to use it outside lsa().

Usage

lsa_ipf(obs, structure = NULL, tol = 1e-08, max_iter = 200L)

Arguments

obs

Square numeric matrix of observed transition counts.

structure

Square 0/1 matrix of the same size: 0 marks a structural zero, 1 an estimable cell. Default NULL: every cell is estimable, which gives the ordinary independence table.

tol

Convergence tolerance on the largest difference between fitted and observed totals (default 1e-8).

max_iter

Maximum number of row-and-column passes (default 200).

Value

A list with the fitted K x K expected-count matrix (fit), the number of passes used (iterations), whether the totals converged within max_iter (converged), and the largest remaining difference between fitted and observed totals (max_margin_diff).

Conditions

Errors carry the class lagdynamics_error and one of:

  • lagdynamics_bad_input: obs contains missing, infinite or negative values.

  • lagdynamics_ipf_infeasible: a row or column has observed transitions but every one of its cells is a structural zero.

References

Wickens, T. D. (1989). Multiway contingency tables analysis for the social sciences (pp. 107-112). Lawrence Erlbaum.

See also

lsa() and its loops and structural_zeros arguments.

Examples

obs <- matrix(c(0, 4, 6,
                3, 0, 5,
                7, 2, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
# Every cell estimable: the ordinary independence table
lsa_ipf(obs)
#> $fit
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] 3.703704 2.222222 4.074074
#> [2,] 2.962963 1.777778 3.259259
#> [3,] 3.333333 2.000000 3.666667
#> 
#> $iterations
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $max_margin_diff
#> [1] 0
#> 

# Self-transitions forbidden: zero expected counts on the diagonal,
# observed row and column totals kept
lsa_ipf(obs, structure = 1 - diag(3))
#> $fit
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] 0.000000 3.104423 6.895577
#> [2,] 3.895577 0.000000 4.104423
#> [3,] 6.104423 2.895577 0.000000
#> 
#> $iterations
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $max_margin_diff
#> [1] 4.908683e-09
#>
